answer:
**Short answer:** The vault has no churn benchmark from Hormozi. It doesn't give a "good" monthly percentage or a point at which to start worrying. What it does have is one real example of him fixing cancellations in a paid community, and his advice that a $100/month community should also offer much more expensive tiers.

**What he's said**
- **The top reason people cancelled his community was overwhelm, not a lack of value.** He was describing Skool Games: "the number one reason that people were cancelling was overwhelm. It was not oh I need to provide more value. It was I need to provide more value per second in fewer total seconds." ([yt--JLN1d1ZKUU @ 11:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=662s), May 2025)
- **His rule for what to add:** "you only introduce something when it's required or necessary for that person to get the the desired value" ([@ 11:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=695s)). Members who face "so many things I have to do… then they leave."
- **Don't rely on the base subscription alone:** "even if you're on school, you have a community, you charge 100 bucks a month, whatever it is, have something that's $1,000 a month. Have something that's $10,000 one time." ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 9:47–10:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=587s), Dec 2025). In his example the expensive tier earns three-quarters of the profit, even though it sells to far fewer people.
- **Monetization:** if customers cost too much to get, he says to make more from each one, through how you charge and collect ([yt-tGhe3sBuk34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34), 2025).

**What he's done:** When overwhelm drove cancellations in Skool Games, he cut three weekly calls to one. He moved the big content drop from monthly to quarterly and turned off app features, so new members had fewer things to do.

**Where this is uncertain:** No source in the vault gives a churn number, a benchmark, or a rule for when to worry. The Skool Games example has no before-and-after figures. Both 2025 videos also promote his own funnel (see the profile's conflict-of-interest notes). Hormozi has probably talked about churn and lifetime value elsewhere, but none of that material is in this vault.

**Extrapolation** (my reasoning from his principles, not something he said)
- **He'd probably reject a single "good churn %" and ask whether churn is your constraint.** His focus-on-one-thing principle says to find the one thing that, if fixed, makes the other problems shrink. Churn is worth worrying about when it caps your growth. In practice, that's when the members you lose each month are about as many as you can add, so the community stops growing however much you market it.
- **He'd tell you to measure inputs, not average outputs.** Find out why people leave (exit surveys, the reasons they give when they cancel) and when they leave. His Skool example points to the first weeks: overwhelmed new members quit before they get any value.
- **His first fix would be to remove things, not add them.** Strip onboarding down to the single action that gets a new member the result they joined for. Bonus calls and content come later.
- **He'd also lower the damage from churn with the money model.** Add the $1,000/month and $10,000 one-time tiers, so revenue doesn't depend only on keeping $100/month members.

Any specific churn threshold, such as "worry above X% a month," would be my number, not his. If you want a grounded answer to that, the vault needs sources where he discusses churn or lifetime value directly. I can look for those and add them.

**Short answer:** Nothing in the vault answers this directly. Going by his principles and his own history, he would most likely tell you to take **revenue**. Profit is a number the client controls and you can't check, while revenue is much harder to shrink. A better move is not to depend on either alone: ask for a guaranteed fee plus a share.

**What the vault actually has (direct sources)**
Hormozi never talks about profit share versus revenue share for consultants in these sources. These are the closest points:

- **He lost everything to a partner he couldn't verify.** He put all the money from selling his gyms into a joint launch. The partner then accused him of skimming, and Hormozi ended up printing the bank statements to go through them "line by line." His lesson: *"when experience meets money money gets the experience and experience gets money"* (Diary of a CEO, 2023: [19:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=1146s), [19:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=1179s)).
- **Leverage is what you get out compared with what you put in.** *"understanding how to get more for what you put in is the game overall"* ([1:44:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=6248s)). Each big jump in his income came from owning a piece of the upside rather than selling hours.
- **When he takes upside himself, he takes ownership.** Acquisition.com usually buys *"minority Stakes 25 to 49 is percent"* ([33:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=2038s)). That comes with real rights and visibility into the books, which a consultant's profit share doesn't.

**Where this is uncertain:** The vault has only 6 sources, and none covers consulting pay deals. His own business (Acquisition.com) is partly paid through profit-type returns, but as an owner with control, not as an outside consultant.

**Extrapolation** (my reasoning from the principles above, not something he said)
- **Revenue over profit.** Profit sits below every decision the client makes: owner salaries, new hires, "marketing expenses," and accounting choices. You don't control any of those. His partner story is exactly the risk you'd face: you depend on their books and have to argue about them afterwards. Revenue is a single figure that's hard to fiddle.
- **Expect a smaller percentage.** A fair revenue share is much lower than a fair profit share. If they offer 20% of profit, don't expect 20% of revenue. Work out what each would pay you in dollars, using their real margins.
- **Match the number to what you change.** If your work grows sales (offers, leads, pricing), revenue measures your impact. If your work cuts costs, profit is the honest measure. In that case, only accept it with clear definitions, a cap on what counts as an expense, and the right to audit.
- **Don't work only for a share.** His "pull cash forward" idea (from the vault's money-models page) would point to a guaranteed fee plus a percentage. That way, a client's bad quarter, or bad faith, doesn't leave you working for nothing.

My own view: unless they offer a clearly better deal, I'd push for a fee plus a revenue share based on growth above their current baseline. That pays you for what you actually add, not for revenue they were already making.

**Short answer:** No source in the vault directly addresses "raise money or bootstrap?" for a first business. What he does say leans clearly toward bootstrapping. Have one small, high-priced, unscalable offer (usually your own time) pay your bills, and put every other dollar into growth. In his framework, capital is a later rung of leverage that you add after you've already built labor and media leverage.

**What he's said**
- **His stated bootstrap method:** "be willing to take 5 10% of your time, charge 10 times more and make enough income from that that you can take all the other money and go aggressive". He presents this as "the bootstrap strategies to growing a big business". Selling time one-on-one "can allow you to live on this and then cash flow all the growth" ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 15:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=919s), Dec 2025).
- **Unscalable is fine at the start:** "it doesn't have to be scalable" ([@ 2:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=129s)). Your own time also lets you "beta test ideas" before the scalable version is figured out ([@ 4:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=297s)), and "If you trade your time for the money, you have a 100% margin" ([@ 6:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=360s)).
- **Customers fund growth:** the purpose of a money model is to "pull cash forward accelerate cash conversion uh within a business so that you can scale". The aim is "to spend as much money as humanly possible uh while maintaining break even or better" ([yt-tGhe3sBuk34 @ 8:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=497s), 2025).
- **Capital comes later in his leverage ladder:** his income went from four figures a month as an employee, to five when self-employed, six once he hired people, seven with licensing (media), and only reached eight with capital ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:43:01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=6181s), 2023). He does treat other people's money as real leverage: "Facebook had other people's money … Max leverage" ([@ 1:45:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=6313s)). He also lists "degrees of capital": friends and family, then institutional, then public ([@ 1:45:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=6347s)).
- **Keep your downside capped:** "when you have a a capp downside, an uncapped upside, that is the recipe for opportunity" ([yt-XGm2ERU9qtA @ 15:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=909s)). If rent is due, get above water first with multiple jobs or a side thing ([@ 17:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1073s)).

**What he's done**
- At his first gym, one personal-training client paid in cash covered his own living costs, so he could put all the gym's money into growth ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 1:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=97s)).
- He went from about $1,000 left in December 2016 to Gym Launch, funded by sales: $60k in one day, then about $26M top line in 12 months. There was no outside raise in the story ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 18:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=1114s), [@ 28:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=1704s)).
- The money he lost was lost through other people: a partner already indicted for fraud emptied the account, and a payment processor froze six months of funds.
- He later sold to private equity (two-thirds stake for $46.2M) after the businesses were already profitable. Acquisition.com now *is* the investor, buying 25–49% stakes.

**Where this is uncertain**
- He never directly compares VC to bootstrapping in these six sources. His examples are service, licensing and info businesses with near-zero cost of goods, where customer cash can fund growth. Capital-heavy businesses such as hardware or deep tech aren't covered.
- He has a conflict of interest. He runs an investment firm, and the "If I Started A Business in 2026" video feeds his Acquisition.com funnel.

**Extrapolation** (my reasoning from his principles, not something he said)
For a first business he'd almost certainly say bootstrap. He'd tell you to:
1. Sell something expensive to a few people, probably your own time at 10x what feels comfortable.
2. Build an offer and money model good enough that customers fund your marketing.
3. Treat raising money as a way to add leverage once you have a working engine, not as a substitute for having one.

His "ignorance is the biggest debt" and "you are the constraint" ideas point the same way. Your first business is mostly how you learn to sell and build offers, and investor money doesn't teach either skill. The exception he'd likely allow is a business that can't physically get started without capital. Even then, his capped-downside rule suggests he'd want the smallest raise possible, and only after customers have paid you.

My own view: this fits most first businesses, but it's the wrong default if you're building something venture-scale like software or hardware, where speed to market matters more than early profit.

I've read the vault's work, focus, sales and pricing pages. Here's the answer.

**Short answer:** Nothing in the vault gives a daily schedule, so the hour-by-hour plan at the end is my extrapolation. What he has said points one way. Your workday should be built around fixing the one thing that's stopping the business from making more money, and most of your hours should go to direct revenue work you can count, like outreach, sales calls and offers. Learning, tweaking and side projects come last. As for how many hours, he works all the time, and in 2025 he says people without responsibilities should work as many hours as they can.

**What he's said**

- **Start by finding the constraint.** Asked how someone becomes a millionaire, he says "we have to identify what the constraint of the of the system is" ([DOAC 2023 @ 1:30:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5419s)). "Growing" just means "get more customers make them worth more" ([@ 35:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=2137s)).
- **Pick one thing and point everything at it.** Ask "what one thing if it were true 12 months from now would change everything for our business" ([Less is More 2025 @ 3:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=232s)). Then "sometimes you have to let the little fires burn" ([@ 6:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=364s)). He also warns that "the easiest way to screw up a project like this is to give it too much time" ([@ 12:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=760s)).
- **Know your inputs.** "if you do not know the inputs that are going to get the output that you want then what are you doing" ([DOAC @ 38:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=2338s)).
- **Volume beats cleverness.** "you just have to do so much volume that it is unreasonable that you fail" ([15 Brutal Truths 2025 @ 9:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=544s)). He wants that volume packed into as few calendar days as possible: "if you can condense how how long that takes you in terms of calendar days not hours um you can get there faster" ([DOAC @ 40:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=2435s)).
- **Consuming content isn't work.** "if you watch more videos, but your conditions are the same and your behavior does not change, you entertained yourself" ([15 Brutal Truths @ 5:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=339s)).
- **Hours.** "if you're under 30 and you have no responsibilities, I recommend working as many hours per week as humanly possible" ([@ 11:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=712s)). On when to stop: "I work until I can't work meaning like my put per unit of time starts to drop precipitously" ([DOAC @ 1:09:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=4168s)).
- **If the money is short now,** sell your own time at a premium, but cap it: "be willing to take 5 10% of your time, charge 10 times more and make enough income from that that you can take all the other money and go aggressive" ([If I Started in 2026 @ 15:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=919s)).
- **Don't keep switching.** "the effort that it takes to compound is the length of time you have to say no to everything else" ([15 Brutal Truths @ 22:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1378s)).

**What he's done:** At his first gym he taught every class and also ran sales consults at 8, 9, 10 and 11 p.m. for about six months ([DOAC @ 55:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=3305s)). When he was short on cash, one high-paying personal-training client covered his living costs, so all of the gym's money could go back into growth ([2026 video @ 1:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=97s)).

**Where this is uncertain**
- His advice to work as many hours as possible depends on your situation. In 2023 he refused to tell anyone how much they "should" work. In 2025 he limits the push to unhappy people under 30 with no responsibilities. If you have kids, he says you have trade-offs but also more experience, so you can spend your effort more strategically ([@ 12:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=744s)).
- Several of these videos also promote his own funnel (a scaling roadmap and a book launch).

**Extrapolation (my reasoning, not something he said)**

These principles suggest a day like this:

1. **Write today's number first.** Before doing anything else, set a count for the input that fixes your constraint. For example, "50 outreach messages, 5 sales calls." If you can't name the constraint, spending the first week finding it is your job.
2. **Do revenue work in the morning, before anything else.** Outreach, sales calls, and improving or raising the price of your offer. This should be most of the day.
3. **Fulfillment fits around sales, not the other way round.** Keep premium one-on-one work to a capped block if you need it to cover your bills.
4. **The leftover time goes to "little fires":** admin, tools, the website and courses. Keep it short and late in the day. Learning only counts if you use it the next day.
5. **Stop when your output drops, not at a set hour.** Then review: did the inputs happen, and did they move the number?
6. **Don't start a second project.** Keep the same main focus until the numbers say it's working or clearly failing.

My own note: his "maximum hours" advice is personal philosophy, and the profile in the vault flags it as such. The part that's backed by his business record is the focus on the constraint and on input volume.

I checked every source in the vault, and Alex Hormozi never says anything there about paying down business debt. The only time "debt" comes up is "the biggest debt all of us pay is ignorance," which is a metaphor. So the first part below is what he has actually said, and the verdict at the end is **extrapolation** from it.

**Short answer (extrapolation):** He'd probably ask whether you have a proven way to turn a dollar into more than a dollar, at a better return than the debt's interest rate. If you do, keep paying the debt on schedule and put the cash into growth. If you don't, the cash isn't "growth money," so pay down the debt, especially if it's expensive or personally guaranteed.

**What he has said that applies**
- **Put spare cash into growth, at break-even or better.** On his 2025 book launch: "the goal is to spend as much money as humanly possible uh while maintaining break even or better" ([2025 launch vlog, "My final update"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=497s) @ 8:17). The aim of a money model, in his words, is to "pull cash forward accelerate cash conversion uh within a business so that you can scale" (same spot).
- **He funded growth with spare cash, not by saving it.** He covered his own living costs with one premium client so he could put all the gym's money back into the gym. His advice: "make enough income from that that you can take all the other money and go aggressive" ([Dec 2025](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=919s) @ 15:19; [story](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=97s) @ 1:37).
- **Get out of trouble first, when you're in it.** "this is why I'm such an advocate of like get yourself out of the hole as fast as humanly possible" ([Nov 2025](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1073s) @ 17:53). Context matters: he's talking about personal survival ("if rent is due"), not business debt. Your profitable business isn't "in the hole," but this would apply if the debt is weighing on you personally.
- **Capped downside, uncapped upside.** "when you have a a capp downside, an uncapped upside, that is the recipe for opportunity" ([Nov 2025](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=909s) @ 15:09).
- **Make one bet and fund it fully.** Pick the one thing that would change everything in 12 months. Splitting money across several fixes "ends up just pulling resources from the one way that I know will work" ([May 2025](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=264s) @ 4:24).

**What he has done**
- In 2016 a partner emptied the bank account and a payment processor froze six months of his funds. By December he had $1,000 left ([Diary of a CEO, 2023](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=1114s) @ 18:34 and 21:19). He knows from experience what happens to a business with no cash cushion.

**Where this is uncertain**
- None of these sources covers interest rates, loans, or how big a cash reserve should be. Everything below is my reasoning from the principles above.
- His advice also promotes his own funnel and books (Acquisition.com, *Money Models*), so he leans toward "grow aggressively."

**Extrapolation:** what he'd likely tell you
1. **Check whether "growth" means something specific.** Do you have a lead channel or offer where $1 in reliably brings back more than $1 fairly quickly, and only needs more cash to scale? If yes, the $60k is fuel. If you can't name that one bet, the cash isn't working, and paying off debt is a guaranteed return.
2. **Compare the returns.** If the debt costs about 8% and your marketing at least pays for itself within a month or two, paying the debt early costs you money. If it's credit-card-style debt at 20% or more, pay it off, because few growth bets beat that reliably.
3. **Don't leave yourself with no cushion.** Given his 2016 experience, he wouldn't put every dollar into either option. Keep enough reserves that a frozen processor or a lost client can't kill the business. The rest goes to the one bet, or to the debt if there's no bet.
4. **Fix the money model before borrowing more or saving.** He'd likely say the faster route is to raise prices or add a premium tier and collect cash earlier, so growth can pay for the debt payoff.

One note of my own: the vault doesn't address taxes, whether you've personally guaranteed the debt, or what the loan terms say. Those details could change the answer more than his philosophy does.

**Short answer:** The vault doesn't cover this. None of the six Hormozi sources gives a refresh schedule or even mentions "ad fatigue." What they do support is a different way to think about it: don't refresh on a calendar. Keep testing new hooks against whatever ad is currently winning, and let the numbers decide when it gets replaced.

**What he's said**
- He thinks the hook or headline matters most, so it's where your testing effort should go. Most funnel tweaks get "20% lift 50% lifts that'd be a monster split test but a banger or killer headline can absolutely outperform the control by two three sometimes 5x" ([14 Years of Marketing Advice @ 0:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=36s)). Experienced advertisers "obsess on the hook they obsess on the headline because they know that's where the money's at" ([@ 1:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=73s)).
- On where new hooks come from: "look at your organic content or other people's organic content or other people's ads look at the first 3 seconds visually and verbally" ([@ 1:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=111s)). He also suggests borrowing from other industries: "can I steal like an artist from a different industry" ([@ 2:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=146s)).
- On copy that doesn't go stale: if you describe the customer's specific moment, "you can always have fresh copy that sounds different and interesting" ([@ ~18:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=1087s)).
- On how far to push spend, during his 2025 book launch: "the goal is to spend as much money as humanly possible uh while maintaining break even or better" ([My final update @ 8:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=497s)).

**What he's done:** In the launch vlog, his team pulls "every hook that's been working for the existing winners, plus a bunch of the organic ones that did well." They wait for data with "a little more statistical significance" before turning around new ad creative for the next shoot ([@ 0:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=33s), [@ 2:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=167s)). Those lines are spoken by staff, not clearly by Hormozi, so treat them as how his company works, not as his own words.

**Where this is uncertain:** The vault has no number for how often to refresh: no days, no frequency cap, no CTR-decay threshold. It's also pre-2026 and drawn from only six videos. His leads book (*$100M Leads*) isn't in the vault and may well address this directly.

**Extrapolation** (not in the sources; my reasoning from his principles above)
- He'd likely reject the question as framed. Asking "how often" treats refreshing as maintenance. His view is that results come from the amount of work you put in, so he'd tell you to keep a steady stream of new hooks running against your current winner all the time. When a new hook beats the control, it replaces the control.
- The trigger is performance, not the calendar. Retire an ad when it can no longer run at break-even or better at the spend you want, and not before. A winner that's still profitable stays on.
- Change the hook first. If the headline is where the 2–5x is, new hooks on a proven body and offer is the cheapest refresh with the biggest payoff. A full rewrite only makes sense when the offer or angle itself has stopped working.
- Refill the pipeline from organic content: post often, watch which first 3 seconds perform, and turn those into ad hooks.

My one disagreement: in practice you still need some cadence so the pipeline never runs dry, for example a set number of new hooks tested every week, with the size set by your budget. That's my suggestion, not his.

I've read the vault's pricing pages and searched the raw transcripts, so here's the answer.

**Short answer:** Based on what's in the vault, he'd tell you not to keep prices where they are. When customers buy a fixed supply faster than you can serve them, he says that should push you to raise prices. Fear of hurting your close rate is the kind of "limiting belief" he says stops people doing it. No source in the vault talks about close rates as a pricing signal, though. That part is extrapolation and is labelled below.

**What he's said (from the vault)**

- **Demand should push prices up.** "when you have demand, cut supply." He says a limited supply "forces, as long as you don't have limiting beliefs, which is why I'm trying to make this for you, it forces you to raise your price." ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=328s) @ 5:28, Dec 2025)
- **The craftsman with demand.** "you have demand because you're so good at it you can either raise the price and just continue to keep raising the prices until eventually become Versace of of of wallets and you make tons of profit but you don't have tons of units". He calls that a valid path. ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5386s) @ 1:29:46, 2023)
- **Offer a tier at 10x.** "the middle is where people die." He says: "If they want to pay you more money, you should give them the opportunity to do so." The expensive tier "literally increases the perceived value" of the cheaper one. In his worked example, 10 buyers out of 100 on the 10x tier bring in about three-quarters of the profit. ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=425s) @ 7:05–9:47)
- **Say the price and stay quiet.** "You must confront the high price." … "We shut up. We let them talk." Anyone who balks can be offered a smaller version. (same video @ 8:09–8:41)
- **Sell to customers who value it most.** "solve rich people problems". At a PR firm he invested in, 15% of customers bought the top package. They rebuilt the business around that niche and charged 10x, and email response rates went up. ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5591s) @ 1:23:11–1:38:38)
- **What a premium tier contains.** Speed ("take whatever the delivery time you currently have is and cut it in half"), priority ("You will always be first in line"), and taking work off the customer. (Dec 2025 video @ 16:25–17:00)

**Where this is uncertain**

- In one 2025 talk he files "improve your sales close rate" and "bumped your … margin" under everyday "sausage making", not the big changes. In that talk he wants owners to look for one change that grows the business many times over ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=595s) @ 9:55). Price matters to him, but he might push you to think bigger than a price tweak.
- The pricing material comes mostly from a December 2025 video that also promotes his Acquisition.com funnel. Its examples are about solo service sellers and new businesses, not a $1.2M crew-based home-services company.
- Whatever he may have said elsewhere about high close rates meaning you're underpriced, it isn't in this vault's sources, so I haven't presented it as his.

**Extrapolation** (my reasoning from the principles above, not something he said)

- **82% is a demand signal.** Most people you inspect say yes, which suggests the price is well below what the value is worth to them. On his "when you have demand… raise your price" logic, protecting the close rate means protecting the discount.
- **The maths favours a price rise.** Take a 20% increase. Your costs are 62% of today's revenue. Profit only drops if the close rate falls below a certain point:
  - If all your costs scale with each job, that point is about **54%**.
  - If all your costs are fixed, it's about **68%**.
  - Your real point is somewhere between the two. For example, if the close rate fell from 82% to 70%, profit would rise by about 30% under the per-job cost assumption, and you'd do fewer jobs. These are rough numbers from your margin, not a forecast.
- **How he'd probably have you do it:**
  1. Raise the base price for new inspections and watch the close rate for a few weeks.
  2. Add a premium tier at several times the price, for example whole-system cleaning plus dryer vent, sanitizing, before-and-after camera footage, guaranteed scheduling within 48 hours and priority service for a year. Quote it first as the anchor, then stay quiet.
  3. Point your marketing at the customers who already buy your biggest jobs, such as larger homes and allergy or asthma households.
  4. Keep raising prices until the close rate stops looking like a bargain.

**My own view:** test the increase in stages rather than all at once. In home services, reviews and referrals can depend on feeling like a fair deal, and the numbers above don't capture that risk.

**Where this is uncertain:** This vault has only six sources. It includes none of the material from his leads book, which is where he'd talk about channels and ads. He runs ads at very large scale (tens of millions a year across his companies), so "never run ads" is clearly not his view. The question is when, and his stated test (ads that at least pay for themselves) needs numbers you don't have yet.

**Extrapolation** (my reasoning from the principles above, not his words)

1. **Your bottleneck is probably not leads.** You have a channel that works: 1 sale per 20 doors. Ads would be a second fix running alongside a first one that's already working, which is the thing he warns against. The one thing to bet on is more doors per week, and eventually a second person knocking who shadows you and does twice your volume.
2. **Treat repairs as your way in, not your goal.** A $1,500 repair puts you on someone's roof. Make a free full-roof inspection with photos part of every repair. Track how many repair customers you can turn into replacement jobs. One $20k replacement is worth about 13 repairs, so that conversion rate is your "make more from each customer" lever.
3. **Change your door pitch toward replacements.** Choose streets by roof age, by recent storms, and by home value, so you're talking to the people who value a replacement most. Give them an offer they'd "feel stupid saying no to": strong guarantee, fast install, insurance-claim handling, financing. Then measure doors per replacement separately from doors per repair.
4. **Ads come later, with a test.** Once you know your close rate and profit per replacement, you can work out what a lead is worth to you. Then run a small ad test against that number. That's how ads can pay for themselves, which is his rule.

One note of my own (not from the vault): roofing depends heavily on insurance claims, storms and local licensing. None of that is in his material, so check the replacement strategy against how your market actually works.

**Where this is uncertain**

**Extrapolation** (my reasoning from the principles above, not his words)

1. **Find the real reason you stall at $100k.** Under his break-even rule, the limit comes from your numbers, not from Meta. Customer acquisition cost rises as spend grows, and at about $100k a month it passes what a customer pays you in their first stretch. He'd point at the money model first: upsells, a 10x tier, a continuity offer, and getting more cash in the first 30 days. Each dollar you add per customer raises the CAC you can afford, which lets you push Meta further.
2. **Then check the offer and the ads.** If the offer is weak, conversion drops as you reach colder audiences. For the ads, he says to find hooks by copying the first three seconds of content and ads that already work (see the headlines-and-hooks page in the vault).
3. **If you still want a new channel, pick one.** Run affiliates *or* podcasts, give it your best people and a deadline, and let small problems elsewhere wait. Running both at once while also fixing Meta is the overload he warns about. Of the two, affiliates fit better: you pay only when a sale happens, so it scales the same break-even way. That choice is my inference; he doesn't say it in the vault.
4. **Order:** money model first, because it makes every channel more profitable, including the one you add later. Then one new channel.

My own view, separate from his: with 85% of customers from one platform, you could lose a lot if Meta bans the account or changes its rules. That's a fair reason to start one more channel even if Meta could still scale. The vault doesn't show Hormozi addressing that risk.

**Short answer:** No. Hormozi had this exact problem and fixed it the other way round. When overwhelm was the top cancel reason in his own community (Skool Games), he removed calls and content. Your "can't keep up" members are telling you the same thing, and adding bonus trainings and live calls makes it worse.

**What he's said and done**

- **His own case is close to yours.** In his May 2025 talk "Less is More" he described Skool Games: "we had like three a week and then we also had like content was getting dumped in there and basically the number one reason that people were cancelling was overwhelm. It was not oh I need to provide more value. It was I need to provide more value per second in fewer total seconds" ([source @ 11:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=662s)).
- **What he cut:** "we removed two of the three calls, except kept it to one and we moved the big download from once a month to once a quarter so that people could get on top of it". He also turned off app features "so that people would have fewer things to do when they got in" ([@ 11:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=695s)).
- **His rule for adding things:** "you only introduce something when it's required or necessary for that person to get the the desired value" ([@ 11:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=695s)).
- **Subtract first.** "how much can I take away and still have it be good and not only be good but it probably is better" (@ 11:02), and "you can't go deep if you have too many things" ([@ 8:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=529s)).
- **The value equation explains why.** Effort is one of the things that lowers value: "effort are the things that you have to start doing that you don't want to do as a result of this purchase" ([Diary of a CEO, 2023 @ 1:21:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=4864s)). Each extra training or call raises that cost.

**Where this is uncertain**

- The vault covers his response to "overwhelm" only. Nothing in it speaks directly to "too expensive" as a cancel reason, to churn benchmarks, or to whether 30% is normal at $99/month.
- The Skool story comes from one talk, and he gives no before-and-after churn numbers.

**Extrapolation** (not in the sources; built from his principles)

- **"Too expensive" probably means low value, not a high price.** By his value equation, value goes down as effort goes up. A member who can't keep up gets little out of the membership, so $99 feels like too much. More bonuses would add effort and push that further. Fixing overwhelm should reduce both cancel reasons.
- **Apply his tests to your offer:**
  - Ask "If we only did this one thing, would we accomplish all of our goals?" ([@ 3:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=200s)). Find the one result members joined for and build the membership around it.
  - Go through the member experience and "take a note every time you have to do something" (from his December 2025 talk on premium offers), then cut those steps.
  - Release content in stages so new members aren't hit with the whole library on day one, as he did with the quarterly download.
- **Offer a higher tier rather than piling on bonuses.** He says "the middle is where people die" and that every business should list an offer at 10x its main price. If some members want more calls, put them in a separate premium tier, maybe one-on-one or a small group. That way the base $99 tier gets simpler, and the people who want more can pay for it.
- **Check your exit data first.** If "can't keep up" members drop off in their first 30 to 60 days, that points strongly to overwhelm, which supports cutting rather than adding.

One caveat on the source: the talk was posted on his own channel, and its description opens with an Acquisition.com lead magnet, so treat it as partly marketing. The Skool Games example is still a hands-on report of a change he made, not just theory.
